title: Thalassemia
covers: What thalassemia is and how it is inherited, the α and β forms from carrier to transfusion-dependent disease, telling trait from iron deficiency, and treatment: transfusion, chelation, transplant, gene therapy and the newer drugs.

items.p: An autosomal recessive microcytic anemia caused by reduced or absent globin chain synthesis. Carriers are common across the Mediterranean, the Middle East and Asia.

ul: Globin imbalance: too few β (or α) chains, so the unpaired partner chains precipitate
Ineffective erythropoiesis: the marrow makes red cell precursors, but most die before they mature
Hemolysis: the damaged cells that do reach the blood are destroyed early

items.p: The lecturer marked the β-thalassemia pathway as very important. Anemia raises erythropoietin; the marrow expands, which deforms bone and increases iron absorption from the gut. Transfusions add more iron. The result is iron overload.

table: Two from each parent; usually deletions

ul: Transfusion-dependent (TDT, formerly β-thalassemia major): regular transfusion to survive
Non-transfusion-dependent (NTDT): β-thalassemia intermedia, HbH disease, moderate HbE/β-thalassemia
Minor: the carrier (heterozygote) state

items.p: Two carriers have a 25% chance of an affected child, 50% of a carrier and 25% of an unaffected child in every pregnancy. Consanguinity raises the risk.

summary.h: α-thalassemia by number of genes lost

table: Hydrops fetalis; fatal without treatment in the womb

items.p: HbH is four β chains. Hb Bart's is four γ chains.
HbH disease flares with fever, infection or oxidant drugs. Diagnosis: HbH inclusions on a supravital stain and an HbH peak on electrophoresis or HPLC. Non-deletional forms are more severe.
The carrier has a mild microcytic anemia that is often mistaken for iron deficiency. The key finding is HbA2 above 3.5%.

ul: Iron deficiency can lower HbA2 and hide the trait: recheck HbA2 after iron is replaced
No treatment, and no iron unless iron deficiency is proven
Genetic counseling for the patient and partner

items.p: Appears at 6–24 months, when fetal γ chains switch off. Pallor, poor feeding, irritability, failure to thrive, jaundice and a large liver and spleen. Without treatment, death usually comes in the first decade.
Under-treated children develop frontal bossing, maxillary overgrowth, a hair-on-end skull X-ray, growth failure, delayed puberty and fractures. Adequate transfusion from infancy prevents this.

ul: Blood count: very low hemoglobin, low MCV and MCH
Smear: microcytosis, target cells, nucleated red cells, basophilic stippling, teardrop cells
Electrophoresis: very high HbF; HbA absent in β⁰ and low in β⁺
DNA studies: identify the mutations for counseling and prenatal diagnosis

items.note: On slide 3 the handwritten label "reticulocytes" points at a cell with a nucleus. A reticulocyte has no nucleus; the cell looks like a nucleated red cell. Worth checking with the lecturer.

items.p: TIF 2025 targets: pre-transfusion hemoglobin 9.5–10.5 g/dL (10–11 with heart disease or extramedullary hematopoiesis), a transfusion every 2–5 weeks, post-transfusion hemoglobin below 13–15 g/dL.
The blood is leukocyte-reduced and matched at least for ABO, Rh and Kell. Irradiation is for specific indications only.
Once transferrin is saturated, non-transferrin-bound iron loads the heart, liver, pancreas, pituitary, thyroid, parathyroid and gonads.

table: Subcutaneous or IV infusion, 5–7 nights a week

ul: Start after 10–20 transfusions or ferritin above 1000 ng/mL
Ferritin at least every 3 months; yearly MRI from age 8–10 for liver iron and cardiac T2*
Monitor the heart (iron cardiomyopathy, arrhythmias), endocrine glands (short stature, delayed puberty, hypothyroidism, diabetes, hypoparathyroidism), bone and liver
Stem cell transplant: offer early, before iron damage, when an HLA-identical donor exists. Risks: graft-versus-host disease, graft failure, infertility.
Gene therapy uses the patient's own stem cells after myeloablation, so there is less immunosuppression and graft-versus-host disease. Lecturer's note: very expensive, highly successful.

table: Lentiviral vector adds a working β-globin gene
CRISPR editing turns fetal hemoglobin back on

items.p: TIF 2025: gene therapy is the best option from age 14, or when there is no HLA-identical sibling donor.

ul: Luspatercept: traps TGF-β family ligands that block late red cell maturation. 1 mg/kg under the skin every 3 weeks, adults. Watch blood pressure and clots, especially after splenectomy.
Mitapivat: an oral pyruvate kinase activator for adults with α- or β-thalassemia.

items.p: β-thalassemia intermedia has a later onset and a milder chain imbalance. Iron overload still develops, from increased gut absorption, even without transfusion.

ul: Complications: thrombosis (especially after splenectomy), pulmonary hypertension (screen with echocardiography), bone disease, extramedullary masses, leg ulcers, gallstones
Transfuse for a defined goal, then reassess: poor growth or delayed puberty, anemia that affects daily life, a growing spleen, complications, surgery, pregnancy, infection
Monitor iron with liver iron on MRI, not ferritin alone. Chelate at liver iron of 5 mg Fe/g or more, or ferritin of 800 ng/mL or more

items.p: HbE/β-thalassemia (HbE is a β26 Glu→Lys variant, common in Southeast Asia): mild at hemoglobin 9–12, moderate at 6–7 (NTDT), severe at 4–5 g/dL (TDT).

Splenectomy is done less often than before. Indications: massive spleen or hypersplenism, rising transfusion needs despite adequate therapy, or failure to thrive when transfusion and chelation are unavailable.

ul: Vaccinate first: pneumococcal, meningococcal, Hib. Penicillin afterwards.
Risks: overwhelming sepsis, thrombosis, pulmonary hypertension

items.p: Prevention: community awareness, premarital screening, genetic counseling, prenatal and preimplantation diagnosis.

ul: First national report: 425 patients, 66% TDT and 34% NTDT, spread evenly across the country
Parents were first-degree relatives in 53%
21 mutations found; IVSI-110 is the most common
Transplant programs: 40 children with a projected 5-year survival of 90%; national program, 10 children, all cured
